title: Two senses of moral good
source_text: THESIS I. DE necessitate gratiae, & de viribus liberi arbitrii, in natura hominis per peccatum corrupta, circa bonum morale, magna est in Schola Romana sententiarum varietas. Ad cujus intelligentiam observandum est in Scholis bonum morale aliquando latius, aliquando strictius sumi. Bonum morale late sumptum significat omne illud quod sic a voluntate & ratione pendet, & utramque afficit, ut propterea homini praemium, vel laus aliqua debeatur, & ejus respectu homo simpliciter bonus denominari possit. Adeoque bonum illud totum situm est in virtute & actionibus secundum virtutem, sive virtus illa sit acquisita, sive infusa, sive ordinis naturalis, sive ordinis supernaturalis.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. Concerning the necessity of grace, and concerning the strength of free choice, in the nature of man corrupted by sin, about moral good, there is great variety of opinions in the Roman School. For the understanding of which it is to be observed that in the Schools moral good is taken sometimes more widely, sometimes more strictly. Moral good taken widely signifies all that which so depends on the will and reason, and affects both, that on that account a reward or some praise is owed to man, and in respect of it man can be called good simply. And so that good is wholly placed in virtue and in actions according to virtue, whether that virtue be acquired or infused, whether of the natural order or of the supernatural order.
pass_b_english: On the necessity of grace and the strength of free choice in human nature corrupted by sin, with respect to moral good, opinions in the Roman School vary widely. To understand this variety we must note that the Schools use 'moral good' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense.

In the wider sense, moral good is everything that depends on will and reason and shapes them both in such a way that a man is owed praise or reward for it and can be called good without qualification. So that good lies entirely in virtue and in acts done according to virtue, whether the virtue is acquired or infused, natural or supernatural.
